books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Lecompton Constitution, Article VII, Section 1 (1857). Public domain. Wording verified against the excerpts at the Harry S. Truman Library (trumanlibrary.gov, Lecompton Constitution lesson).
stimulus.text: The right of property is before and higher than any constitutional sanction, and the right of the owner of a slave to such slave and its increase is the same and as inviolable as the right of the owner of any property whatever.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Lecompton fight best shows that popular sovereignty failed because

options.text: Kansas had too few settlers to hold a vote.
options.misconception: Kansas had thousands of settlers; the problem was the vote’s design, not its size.

options.text: the Supreme Court had banned all voting there.
options.misconception: The Court never banned voting in Kansas; the Lecompton convention rigged the vote itself.

options.text: Douglas himself supported the Lecompton Constitution.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Douglas broke with Buchanan over Lecompton; he never supported it.

options.text: voters were given no fair way to reject the constitution.

rationales.A: Kansas had thousands of settlers; the problem was the vote’s design, not its size.
rationales.B: The Court never banned voting in Kansas; the Lecompton convention rigged the vote itself.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Douglas broke with Buchanan over Lecompton; he never supported it.
rationales.D: Background from the books: voters could choose the constitution “with slavery” or “without slavery,” but never reject it outright.
rationales.general:
1. Read the choice voters were given: the constitution with slavery, or the constitution without slavery.
2. Notice what was missing: no ballot let them reject the constitution itself.
3. See the fraud: even “without slavery” kept the enslaved people already in Kansas enslaved.
4. Watch the ending: Kansas voters rejected the English Bill offer by 11,300 to 1,788 in August 1858.
Remember: a vote with no real “no” is not a vote; it is a ceremony.
